sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in Lapeer County?
sections.html:
Your township, city or village treasurer sends it, and the county treasurer only gets involved when a bill goes unpaid. Local bills are issued July 1 and December 1, and anything still open after March 1 is passed to the Lapeer County Treasurer as delinquent.

The county covers 663 square miles, of which 643 are land, in the part of Michigan known as the Thumb. Its county seat is the City of Lapeer. Imlay City and Brown City are the other two cities, and the villages are Almont, Clifford, Columbiaville, Dryden, Metamora, North Branch and Otter Lake. Eighteen townships fill in the rest. Because each unit runs its own treasurer and assessor, the first call about a bill always goes to the office for the place where the house sits.

  • Questions about a current bill: the local treasurer. The county treasurer cannot waive local penalties or interest.
  • Value, classification or a principal residence claim: the local assessor.
  • Taxes that turned delinquent after March 1: the County Treasurer in the County Complex at 255 Clay Street, Lapeer.
  • Getting a prior owner's name off a bill: the local assessor, with a deed or other proof of the transfer.

sections.h2: What does the Lapeer County equalization office do?
sections.html:
It checks that assessments are fair between local units, and it does not set the assessment on any one house. The department advises the Board of Commissioners on true cash value and runs annual sales and appraisal studies for each class of property.

That work rests on section 211.34 of the General Property Tax Act, which tells the county board to review each township and city roll for uniformity every year. If your own assessed value looks wrong, take it to the local assessor first. The county office exists to correct gaps between units, such as one township running below the sales level of its neighbors. Public hearings on county operating millage are held in the Commission Chambers at the County Complex, and a notice for a proposed 0.4881 mill increase on 2024 levies shows how those hearings are announced.

sections.h2: What does a late payment cost in Lapeer County?
sections.html:
A late bill picks up a flat administration fee and monthly interest, and the county treasurer has no power to waive them. The schedule below comes from the Lapeer County Treasurer's published FAQ.

ChargeAmountWhen it applies
Administration fee4%Added March 1, when unpaid taxes turn delinquent
Interest, first delinquent year1% per monthCounted from the original due date
Interest after forfeiture1.5% per monthStarts the following March 1 and reaches back to the turnover date
Title search fee$175Added at forfeiture
Recording fees$60Added at forfeiture

Source: Lapeer County Treasurer FAQ, with the rules in MCL 211.56 and 211.78.

The office takes personal checks, cashier's checks, money orders, credit cards and cash, with checks payable to Lapeer County Treasurer. Partial payments are allowed at any time, and a receipt is mailed to the address on the check. Fees and interest keep running on whatever balance remains.

Mortgage servicers sometimes miss a payment. The treasurer's FAQ states that the owner, not the lender, carries the responsibility, so compare each mortgage statement with the local treasurer's records.

sections.h2: How does tax foreclosure work in Lapeer County?
sections.html:
Foreclosure can begin once taxes are two years delinquent, and the county treasurer then sells the property at public auction. A 1999 law, Public Act 123 (MCL 211.78), cut the time owners have to catch up on unpaid bills.

Forfeiture falls on March 1, one year after the turnover date, and it only prepares the parcel for foreclosure. The treasurer's page states plainly that the property is not lost at forfeiture. The later foreclosure is final, and nothing returns the house to the owner afterward.

  • State law requires five notices: two by first class mail, two by certified mail and one by personal service. The county sends another three to five on its own.
  • Names and addresses of delinquent owners are published in the newspaper, and recorded lienholders, mortgage holders and land contract holders are notified.
  • At the first auction the minimum bid equals all taxes, interest and fees. If a parcel does not sell, a very low minimum applies at the second auction.
  • The foreclosure list is normally available around May 1 each year. Mortgage foreclosures are not run by this office.

Anyone behind on taxes who wants to sell should do it before forfeiture, because the $175 and $60 charges and the higher interest rate arrive on that date.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Lapeer County assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the March board of review in the township, city or village where the house stands. Ask the local assessor for the meeting dates, since each unit sets its own.

For residential property the board of review comes first. Under MCL 205.735a, you then file with the Michigan Tax Tribunal by July 31 of the tax year. Commercial and industrial real property can go straight to the Tribunal, with a May 31 filing date. A petition over an arithmetic error on a bill has its own 60 day limit. Owners representing themselves are allowed to appear without an attorney.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can lower a Lapeer County tax bill?
sections.html:
The principal residence exemption is the main one for homeowners. It removes the school district operating levy, up to 18 mills, from a home you own and occupy as a Michigan resident.

  • File Form 2368 with the local assessor. The county FAQ gives June 1 for the summer cycle and November 1 for the winter cycle.
  • A denied claim can go to an informal conference with the Department of Treasury's exemption unit, or to the Tax Tribunal.
  • The poverty exemption is requested at the city or township assessor's office.
  • The county treasurer also accepts financial hardship deferral applications. Ask that office what documents it wants.

The principal residence exemption is separate from the Homestead Property Tax Credit, which is filed with the Michigan income tax return.

sections.h2: What do Lapeer County sellers pay at closing?
sections.html:
The seller pays transfer tax, and the Register of Deeds charges it at $1.10 per $1,000 for the county and $7.50 per $1,000 for the state. On a $200,000 sale that is $220 plus $1,500, or $1,720 together.

Warranty deeds, land contracts and any deed carrying a covenant of warranty also need a tax certificate from the County Treasurer, which costs $5 under MCL 211.135. The recording fee is a separate $30. Current taxes are normally split between buyer and seller by the purchase agreement and the title company's settlement statement. If a prior year is delinquent, get the payoff amount from the County Treasurer before the closing date so interest and fees are counted correctly.

faqs.q: When do Lapeer County property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: Unpaid summer and winter bills turn delinquent after March 1 and move to the Lapeer County Treasurer. That is also the day the 4% administration fee is added and 1% monthly interest is counted from the original due date.

faqs.q: Can the Lapeer County treasurer waive penalties?
faqs.a: No. The treasurer's FAQ says the fees and interest in the property tax act have no waiver provision, and the office cannot remove them. Ask about the financial hardship deferral if a one-time expense caused the delay.

faqs.q: Can I pay a delinquent Lapeer County bill in pieces?
faqs.a: Yes. Partial payments are accepted at any time and a receipt is mailed back. Statutory fees and interest still apply to whatever is left unpaid.

faqs.q: How long before Lapeer County can foreclose on unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Two years from the delinquency. Forfeiture comes a year after turnover on March 1, and foreclosure follows after the notices are served. Foreclosed parcels go to public auction.

faqs.q: Who takes my name off the bill after I sell?
faqs.a: The local assessor in the township, city or village where the house is. The county treasurer has no authority to change a name on a bill, so bring the deed or proof of transfer to the assessor.
